The town of Udayapura, now Udaypur in Vidisha district, takes its name from the Paramara king Udayaditya, who is said to have founded it together with the great temple of Udayesvara.
Udaypur is a village in the Basoda tehsil of Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, a few miles from Basoda railway station, lying on the Malwa plateau north-east of Vidisha.
Udayapura is mentioned in several inscriptions of the Paramara period and in later records, including the Udaipur prasasti, which gives the genealogy of the Paramara kings of Malwa.
Local tradition holds that the temple was built in a single night by divine craftsmen, and villagers tell stories of how the shrine was saved when invaders came to destroy it.
The Udayesvara temple at Udaypur is regarded as the finest surviving example of Paramara architecture and one of the most complete Bhumija temples in India.
Scholars have long debated the date of the foundation of Udayapura and whether the temple was begun in 1059 or completed in 1080, since the inscriptions give differing accounts.

The Betwa rises in the Vindhyan hills and flows north-east through Vidisha district; its tributaries drain the plateau, and the river's discharge varies sharply between the monsoon and the dry season.
The district lies on the Vindhyan plateau, where horizontally bedded sandstones and shales are capped in places by Deccan trap basalt, giving rise to flat-topped hills and fertile black soils.
The climate is characterised by a hot summer and a general dryness except during the south-west monsoon season; the average annual rainfall in the district is about 1,100 mm.
The forests of the district are of the dry deciduous type, with teak, khair and tendu; the fauna includes leopards, nilgai, chital and many species of birds.
The fine-grained sandstone quarried from the nearby hills provided the material for the temple, while the tank and the fertile soil supported the agricultural settlement around it.

Stone tools of the Lower and Middle Palaeolithic have been found along the Betwa and its tributaries, and painted rock shelters in the hills of the district attest to early human habitation.

Vidisha, ancient Vidisa, with its suburb Besnagar, was one of the great cities of early India; the Heliodorus pillar, erected by a Greek envoy, and the nearby stupas of Sanchi testify to its importance under the Mauryas and Sungas.
The region around Vidisa was known in ancient literature as Dasarna, the eastern part of Akara, and is described in the Meghaduta of Kalidasa.

After the Guptas, whose caves at Udayagiri lie near Vidisha, the region passed under the Gurjara-Pratiharas before the rise of the Paramaras of Malwa, who contended with the Kalachuris and Chandellas.
Vidisa stood on the great southern trade route linking Ujjayini with the Gangetic plain, which made it a meeting point of merchants, monks and pilgrims.

The Paramaras claimed descent from a hero born of the sacrificial fire-pit on Mount Abu; their historical founder in Malwa was Upendra, and the dynasty rose to power under Siyaka and Vakpati Munja.
Bhoja, the most celebrated king of the dynasty, ruled from Dhara for about half a century; a great warrior and patron of letters, he is credited with numerous works on poetry, architecture and yoga.

After the death of Bhoja the kingdom was overrun by the Kalachuri Karna and the Chaulukya Bhima; Udayaditya, described in the Udaipur prasasti as a relative of Bhoja, then restored the Paramara power.
Udayaditya defeated Karna with the help of allies, re-established the kingdom of Malwa and founded the town of Udayapura, where he built the temple of Udayesvara.
The Paramara kings were great builders who endowed temples, excavated tanks and granted land to Brahmins, and towns such as Dhara, Bhojpur and Udayapura grew around their foundations.
Udayaditya was succeeded by his sons Lakshmadeva and Naravarman, under whom the kingdom began to decline in the face of Chaulukya attacks.

The temple stands on a high platform within a walled enclosure; it consists of a sanctum, a vestibule and a closed hall with three porches, and the corners of the platform carry small subsidiary shrines.
The spire is of the Bhumija type, with four central bands and rows of miniature spires arranged in horizontal tiers between them, a form that originated in Malwa under the Paramaras.
The wall rests on a series of richly carved mouldings, and the doorway to the sanctum is framed by bands of scrollwork, with river goddesses at its base.
The niches of the wall contain images of Siva in various forms, the goddess Durga, Ganesa and the guardians of the directions, while celestial maidens occupy the recesses between them.
In Saiva Siddhanta thought the temple is the body of Siva, and its plan and spire express the progression from the manifest to the unmanifest.
The Samaranganasutradhara attributed to Bhoja describes the Bhumija prasada in detail, prescribing its proportions, storeys and the arrangement of its miniature spires.

The Udaipur prasasti, a long Sanskrit inscription in verse found at the temple, gives the genealogy of the Paramara kings from Upendra to Udayaditya and records the building of the temple.
The temple carries a long series of inscriptions spanning many centuries, including records of later kings, Persian inscriptions of the Sultanate and Mughal periods, and the names of pilgrims.
One remarkable inscription arranges the letters of the alphabet and grammatical endings in the form of a serpent, a device associated with Paramara learning.
The court of the Paramaras was a centre of Sanskrit learning; Bhoja himself composed works on grammar, poetics and architecture, and the inscriptions are written in polished kavya style.
The inscriptions record grants of land and villages for the maintenance of the temple and its worship, though their dates and claims must be read critically.

The old town was enclosed by a stone wall pierced by several gates, of which a few still stand, and a fort once occupied the higher ground.
Besides the great temple there are several smaller shrines in the town, including Jain temples and ruined Hindu shrines of the Paramara period.
A mosque built during the reign of the Mughal emperor stands in the town, with a Persian inscription recording its construction, and there are several tombs nearby.
The town has a number of stepwells and wells, as well as a large tank, which supplied water to the inhabitants.
The palace and old havelis of the town, with carved stone facades, reflect its prosperity in the late medieval period.
A survey of the town identified dozens of historic structures, of which only the temple is a protected monument.

Saivism flourished under the Paramaras; ascetic orders of the Pasupata and Saiva Siddhanta schools maintained monasteries attached to the great temples of Malwa.
Daily worship at the temple is performed by hereditary priests, and the festival of Mahashivratri draws large crowds of pilgrims from the surrounding villages.
The inscriptions record grants of villages and revenues for the maintenance of worship, lamps and offerings at the temple.
The people of the area are mainly cultivators growing wheat, gram and soybean, relying on wells and the tank for irrigation.
Udaypur was once a market town with a weekly bazaar, and its stone carvers and craftsmen were known throughout the region.

Udaypur is home to Hindu and Muslim communities who have lived side by side for centuries; the population includes Brahmins, traders, cultivators and artisan castes.
The people speak a dialect of Hindi close to Bundeli, with Malvi influence, while Urdu is spoken in some Muslim households.
The main festivals of the town are Mahashivratri, Holi and Diwali, as well as Muharram and Eid, and a fair is held at the temple every year.
The elders of the town tell many stories about its past, of hidden treasure, of the emperor who tried to destroy the temple, and of the goddess who protects the village.
Folk songs are sung at weddings and festivals, and the local cuisine is based on wheat, pulses and seasonal vegetables.

After the conquest of Malwa by Alauddin Khalji the Paramara kingdom came to an end, and Udaypur passed under the Delhi Sultanate and later the independent Sultans of Malwa at Mandu.
In the Mughal period Udaypur was the headquarters of a pargana in the sarkar of Raisen; a mosque was built and Persian inscriptions record the activities of Mughal officials.
In the eighteenth century the region came under the Marathas and later formed part of the Scindia's state of Gwalior; a Maratha officer presented a brass cover for the linga.
Under Gwalior State Udaypur fell within the Bhilsa district, and nineteenth-century travellers described it as a decayed town.
The decline of Udaypur was gradual, as trade routes shifted, patronage ceased and the population moved to the new railway town of Basoda.

The temple was first described by Alexander Cunningham, whose assistant surveyed the site; later the Archaeological Department of Gwalior State documented its inscriptions in its annual reports.
The temple is a monument of national importance protected by the Archaeological Survey of India under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act.
The temple underwent repairs in the early twentieth century under the Gwalior Archaeological Department, and further conservation of the platform and spire was carried out after independence.
INTACH carried out a listing of the historic buildings of Udaypur, documenting dozens of structures of architectural and historical interest.
Encroachment, neglect and unplanned construction threaten the historic fabric of the town, while most structures other than the temple remain unprotected.

Today Udaypur is a large village with a population of several thousand, a school, a health centre and a road connecting it to Ganj Basoda.
Most families depend on agriculture and daily wage labour, and many young people leave for work in the cities.
For the residents the temple is not a monument but a living place of worship, and many families live in houses built against the old walls.
Residents speak of their wish for better roads, jobs and recognition, and of the difficulties created by restrictions on building near protected monuments.
A small number of tourists and scholars visit the temple, but the town lacks facilities for visitors.

We recommend that a heritage zone be declared around the temple, that the stepwells and gates be repaired, and that building regulations be framed in consultation with residents.
Conservation can succeed only if the people of Udaypur see themselves as custodians of their heritage and are involved in decisions about it.
The Archaeological Survey, the state department, INTACH and universities each have a role, and their efforts must be coordinated.
Heritage tourism, if developed carefully with home stays, local guides and crafts, can provide livelihoods for residents without damaging the historic fabric.
Udaypur can once again become a living historic town where heritage and the well-being of its people go hand in hand.
